title: Don't wait to be rich
hook: many would have reached wisdom if they hadn't thought they'd need to be rich first

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epicurus, philosophy in deeds and not in words. Your line was not words, shape. Did you act once on something you believe? Day four hundred fifty-one.

Once the kids are older. Once I pay off the card. Once work calms down. Once I have the right shoes, the right desk, the right app. Then I'll start. Plenty of plans hang on a sentence like that, and the thing they're waiting for keeps moving. Lucilius had one too. He told Seneca he'd devote himself to philosophy properly once he'd put enough money aside to live on. Seneca's seventeenth letter is his reply, and it's not gentle. Today: don't wait to be rich.
screen: `ONCE THE KIDS ARE OLDER.` → `ONCE I HAVE ENOUGH.` → `DON'T WAIT TO BE RICH.`

segments.voice: First, the plan. Lucilius wants to build up savings before he gives himself to the study of how to live. Sounds sensible. Seneca tells him to throw that plan out. If you're wise, he says, hurry toward a sound mind now. Second, the trap. Riches, Seneca says, have shut many people off from wisdom. They meant to get rich first and study how to live afterward, and the afterward never came. The getting-ready becomes the whole life. The money always needs a little more. Third, the light traveler. Then he praises a poor person's freedom. When the war trumpet sounds, the poor know they aren't the ones under attack. When a house is on fire, they look for the way out, not for what to carry. When a poor person sets out to sea, no crowd of servants fills the dock. Hunger, Seneca says, costs little; fussiness costs a lot. And later in the letter: nature asks for very little. If you want room for your mind, Seneca says, either be poor, or live as if you were. He closes with Epicurus, again: for many, getting rich didn't end their troubles; it only changed them. Fourth, the poverty you choose. The study of wisdom, Seneca says, can't do you good without care for simple living, and simple living is a poverty you choose. That choice is open on any budget. A lot of good things can be started today, with what's already in your hands: a notebook instead of a course, a walk instead of a gym, five quiet minutes instead of a retreat.
screen: `FIRST SAVINGS, THEN WISDOM?` · `THE GETTING-READY BECOMES THE LIFE.` · `THE POOR TRAVEL LIGHT.` · `SIMPLE LIVING, CHOSEN.` · then, large: `START POOR.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been waiting to begin until conditions are right. A practice, a project, a conversation, a habit. Name what you've told yourself you need first. Now ask: what could I do with exactly what I have, today? Make it tiny. One page. One phone call. One stretch. Picture yourself doing that tiny first step, with no new equipment, no better week, no permission. Notice how small it is. The bell holds the time.
Simple living. Seneca's seventeenth letter: a poverty you choose, open on any budget, so you don't have to wait to be rich. Today's word.
Your line: start poor. Take the tiny first step you pictured, today, with exactly what's already in your hands. Day four hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Following Seneca, some people begin a practice of reflection or study right away with simple means, rather than waiting for savings, time off or better conditions.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut 'one of the richest men in Rome' (unsourced superlative, and a near-repeat of day 452's 'honest twist') and the teaching of tomorrow's letter; the fourth turn now follows 17.5 (frugality as voluntary poverty); 'almost everyone', 'most good things' and the told feeling in the practice removed; myth and trapdoor now come from Letter 17; On the Happy Life source dropped.

Checked against Gummere (Wikisource), Letter 17: 17.1 Lucilius wants his estate settled first; 17.3 'Riches have shut off many a man from the attainment of wisdom', the trumpet, the cry of fire, and the poor man going to sea with no retinue on the wharves; 17.4 hunger costs little, squeamishness much; 17.5 'either be a poor man, or resemble a poor man'; 17.9 nature demands but little; 17.11 Epicurus on riches as a change, not an end, of troubles. All paraphrased. Reviewer fixes: the earlier draft had sailors throwing cargo overboard in a storm and 'bread and water', neither of which is in Letter 17 (bread and water is Letters 18 and 25), and stated the index line as a counterfactual ('many would have reached wisdom if...') that the letter does not contain; the teach now follows 17.3. The hook and index line keep the outline wording; a Keeper may want the index softened to match.

'One of the richest men in Rome' is a common characterization based on Tacitus (Annals 13.42, Suillius' charge of 300 million sesterces) and Cassius Dio; the figure comes from hostile sources. Confirm the wording is supportable.
On the Happy Life 17–18: Seneca answers the charge that he lives differently from what he teaches; confirm chapter numbers.
